summary: Specifies how defects are mapped and signaled between a pseudowire and the attachment circuits of the end-to-end service it emulates. It standardizes provider edge behavior for ATM, Frame Relay, TDM, and SONET/SDH services carried over MPLS and similar networks.

plainLanguage.summary: When one part of a long cable-like connection breaks, the other parts should learn about it. This sets rules for passing along fault warnings between the middle of the network and the customer ends.

how do pseudowires signal attachment circuit faults
subtitle: How a provider edge router passes fault warnings between a pseudowire and the customer circuit it emulates.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire carries a legacy service such as ATM, Frame Relay or TDM across a packet network. When something breaks on either the customer circuit or the pseudowire, each side needs to hear about it, and without a standard the routers could react in different ways.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four defect states a provider edge (PE) tracks and two OAM modes. For each service type it says when the PE enters or leaves each state and what it MUST then do, such as inserting AIS or RDI, sending a forward or reverse defect indication, or setting a control word bit.
tldr.outcome: PEs from different vendors raise the same alarms and take the same actions for the same failures, for single-segment pseudowires over MPLS, MPLS/IP and L2TPv3/IP networks.

facts.value: 4 (AC receive, AC transmit, PW receive, PW transmit)

sections.title: Why Defects Need Mapping
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) emulates a native service, such as ATM, Frame Relay, TDM or SONET/SDH, across a packet switched network (PSN). At each end a Provider Edge (PE) connects a customer-facing Attachment Circuit (AC) to the PW. This RFC specifies how defects are mapped and notified between the PW and the ACs of the end-to-end emulated service.

Its goal is that there is no ambiguity about the alarms generated and the actions a PE takes in response to specific failure conditions. It is motivated by the requirements in RFC 4377 and RFC 3916.

The scope is limited. It covers PWs of the same type as their ACs, set up with LDP (RFC 4447) or L2TPv3 (RFC 3931), and only single-segment PWs. Ethernet PWs are covered in a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: When a long pretend cable has a break, both ends should know. This document says exactly who tells whom, and what each one does next.

sections.title: Defect Vocabulary and Locations
sections.content:
The RFC uses "defect" and "fault" interchangeably. A forward defect indication (FDI) travels in the same direction as the user traffic that the defect hurts. A reverse defect indication (RDI) travels the opposite way. The words "upstream" and "downstream" are relative to the direction of traffic: a PE is upstream for the traffic it forwards and downstream for the traffic it receives.

Figure 1 of the RFC marks seven places a defect can occur, labelled (a) to (g). They run from the native service network next to PE1, through PE1's AC and PSN interfaces and the PSN itself, to PE2's interfaces and the native network beyond it. The procedures are written from the point of view of PE1.

The RFC also notes that both data plane and control plane defects matter, because a control plane defect can affect PW status even if control messages take a different path from PW traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A warning that goes the same way as the traffic is like shouting down the road ahead. A warning that goes backwards is like telling the people behind you.

sections.title: The Four Defect States
sections.content:
PE1 tracks four defect states, which reflect both directions of the service on both the AC and the PW sides: AC receive, AC transmit, PW receive and PW transmit. The observed state combines defects PE1 detects itself with defects it learns about through notifications.

A receive defect is upstream of PE1 and hurts traffic arriving at PE1. PE1 learns of it from a forward defect indication, or detects it directly. A transmit defect hurts traffic PE1 sends. A PE generally cannot detect transmit defects by itself, so it relies on reverse defect indications from other devices.

If a PE is in both the receive and transmit defect states of the same PW service, the receive defect takes precedence for deciding what actions to take.

For a PW over L2TPv3/IP using only the basic Circuit Status AVP, the PW transmit defect state is not valid. The PE can only enter the PW receive defect state.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of four warning lights: one for each direction of travel on each side of the station. If the incoming light and the outgoing light are both on, the incoming one decides what to do.

sections.title: Two OAM Modes
sections.content:
The RFC defines two modes, which differ in how native service (NS) OAM messages map to PW OAM messages.

In the single emulated OAM loop mode, one end-to-end NS OAM loop is emulated by passing NS OAM messages transparently over the PW. The upstream PE MUST relay NS OAM messages, MUST signal AC defects with an NS defect notification (or a PW defect notification if NS messages cannot be generated), and MUST signal PW defects with a PW defect notification. The downstream PE MUST insert NS defect notifications into its AC when it learns of a PW or remote AC defect. This is the default for all ATM cell mode services and the only mode for CEP and SAToP/CESoPSN TDM services.

In the coupled OAM loops mode, three OAM loops are joined at the AC/PW boundaries and NS OAM messages never cross the PW. The upstream PE MUST terminate a received NS defect notification and translate it into a PW defect notification. This is the default for Frame Relay, ATM AAL5 PDU transport and AAL5 SDU transport, and optional for ATM VCC cell mode.
sections.plainLanguage: In one mode the station just passes the customer's alarm bell along the line. In the other mode it listens to the bell, then rings its own separate bell on the other side.

sections.title: How Defects Are Signaled on the PW
sections.content:
For MPLS and MPLS/IP PSNs where LDP has negotiated the status TLV, a PE MUST use the PW status TLV for AC and PW status and defect notification. It MAY also use VCCV-BFD for fault detection only (CV types 0x04 and 0x10). The RFC maps the indications to PW status code points: a forward defect indication is the logical OR of Local AC (ingress) Receive Fault, Local PSN-facing PW (egress) Transmit Fault and PW Not Forwarding, while a reverse defect indication is the OR of Local AC (egress) Transmit Fault and Local PSN-facing PW (ingress) Receive Fault.

For L2TPv3/IP, a PE SHOULD use the Circuit Status AVP, with the same mapping, and the extended bits of RFC 5641 where supported. Without extended support, the Active bit conveys AC defects and the PE MAY use CDN or StopCCN messages to tear down sessions.

With BFD diagnostic codes, 0, 1, 3 and 7 report BFD session state changes. When CV types 0x08 or 0x20 are used, codes 6 (Concatenated Path Down) and 8 (Reverse Concatenated Path Down) carry forward and reverse indications. These CV types SHOULD NOT be used when the PW is set up by the LDP or L2TP control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: The station has a few kinds of message cards it can send down the line. Each kind of trouble has its own card, and this section says which card to use.

sections.title: Per-Service Procedures
sections.content:
Each service type gets its own entry and exit criteria and its own list of consequent actions.

  • ATM: on entering the PW receive defect state, the PE MUST start inserting AIS into the AC and stop generating CC cells, and MUST send RDI to PE2 if it found the defect without an FDI. On an AC receive defect in coupled mode it MUST send FDI to PE2 and insert RDI cells towards CE1.
  • Frame Relay: on a PW defect the PE MUST clear the Active bit for the FR AC in a full status report. The AC transmit defect state is not valid for a FR AC.
  • TDM (SAToP, CESoPSN, TDMoIP): real-time needs rule out PW status messages, so the PE uses control word flags. It MUST set the R bit in packets sent back to PE2 on a PW receive defect, and MUST set the L bit on an AC receive defect.
  • CEP (SONET/SDH): uses the L, R, N and P bits. A PE enters the PW receive defect state on L bit set, both N and P bits set, or loss of packet synchronization.

In ATM and Frame Relay port mode, the PE does not track individual circuits, so it cannot relay PW defect state. Native timeouts at the customer equipment reveal the failure instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of customer line has its own alarm style, so the station follows a different checklist for each: some use warning signals, some flip a flag on every packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mapping messages do not change the security functions inherent in the actual messages. The generic PW security considerations of RFC 3985 apply to NS OAM messages carried inside the PW, those of RFC 5085 apply to VCCV, and those of RFC 4447 apply to OAM carried in LDP status messages.

Because these mechanisms carry OAM messages and fault conditions between native service networks and PSNs, end-to-end service continuity depends on a trust relationship between the operators of those networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The station trusts the alarm messages it passes along, so the companies running each side must trust each other.
